body.text: The United States, Japan, Australia, and the Philippines have agreed to establish a coordination hub in the Philippines and to synchronize efforts to strengthen the nation’s defenses in the face of China’s growing maritime assertiveness.

In a joint statement released on November 10, the informal security grouping – sometimes known as the “Squad” – committed to several “forward-looking initiatives.” These included the establishment of a Combined Coordination Center in the Philippines and the synchronization of defense investments in order “to support the Philippines in defending its archipelago.”

They also agreed to strengthen ministerial and senior policy-level consultations and expand “the scope, complexity, and frequency of their combined exercises and cooperative activities,” the statement said.

The joint statement came more than a week after the defense ministers from the U.S., Japan, Australia, and the Philippines met in Cebu on the sidelines of the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting Plus, where they committed to greater defense policy coordination. It was the sixth meeting of the four countries’ defense leaders in four years.

The statement did not provide further details on the proposed center’s location or timeline for establishment, nor any details on its specific functions. However, the statement said that the center would build on the Defense Cooperation Council (DCC), a multilateral defense cooperation framework that was established by the four Squad nations. Terms of reference for the DCC were signed by military brass from the U.S., Japan, Australia, and the Philippines in Singapore on May 29.

The DCC framework “provides for information sharing, regular multilateral maritime activities, coordinated strategic communications, and improved interoperability in operational planning, logistics, and military sustainment,” U.S. Pacific Command said in a statement.

All of these developments are a clear response to China’s growing maritime power and assertiveness, a trend that has caused varying degrees of concern in all four Squad nations. For the Philippines, the primary concern is Beijing’s activities in areas of the South China Sea that Manila claims under international law. Over the past four years, Beijing has increased both the frequency and intensity of its incursions into Manila’s exclusive economic zone. This has prompted a series of dangerous confrontations between the two nations, pushing relations to their lowest point in years.

In Tuesday’s joint statement, the Squad defense chiefs “reiterated their serious concerns about the situations in the East China Sea and the South China Sea” and “reaffirmed their strong opposition to any unilateral actions, including by force or coercion, which escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability.”

China’s actions in the South Chinas Sea have already led the Philippines to enhance its security cooperation with all three members of the Squad, as well as other partners including Canada. This has involved joint maritime and coast guard patrols and military exercises known as Maritime Cooperative Activities, the 20th round of which was held between the Philippines, U.S., and Canada in the Sulu Sea in mid-September.

It has also involved the transfer of equipment intended to fortify the Philippines’ defense and deterrence. On this front, Japan announced on November 9 that it would provide a radar system and unmanned aircraft worth 4.3 billion yen ($27 million) to the Philippine military under its Official Security Cooperation framework. The project is of “great importance in further promoting security cooperation between Japan and the Philippines, enhancing security of important sea lanes for Japan, and contributing to maintaining and strengthening regional peace and stability,” Japan’s Foreign ministry said in a statement, as per Kyodo News.

While the exact purpose of the Combined Coordination Center remains unclear, its creation will likely further strengthen and institutionalize the security cooperation between the four Squad nations in the face of China’s behavior.

As Collin Koh, a scholar at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, said in a post on X, “This is certainly [a] more tangible form of support than verbal statements expressi[ng] solidarity with Manila.” He also said it would help “augment” the partners’ Maritime Cooperative Activities in the South China Sea.

The Chinese response has so far been as one would expect. In a post on X, the state-run Global Times tabloid accused the Philippines of becoming “the most convenient tool for the U.S., Japan, and Australia to stir up trouble for China over the South China Sea issue.” It added, “Instead of cheering for the so-called coordination hub, perhaps Manila should take a moment to ponder how to stop being a pawn.”
